ui.2204: There are three models behind seven calculators.
ui.2205: MBA. A points-based admissions model across 43 business schools: 35 on a shared scale and 8 modelled individually. It offers two readings. As published evaluates score benchmarks directly; Corrected scores test thresholds as continuous ranges, which affects Columbia, Stanford, NYU and Yale.
ui.2206: Business master’s. A purpose-built model for pre-experience master’s in Management, Finance and Marketing. It enforces each programme’s hard eligibility rules first (degree requirements, minimum quantitative credits, language level, work-experience caps), then weighs your profile under that school’s own emphasis. Where a school publishes its weights or a points table (St. Gallen, Mannheim, TUM) the model uses them as written.
ui.2207: Computing master’s. A rule-first model for 26 programmes in the UK, Europe and the US across Computer Science, Data Science and AI, and conversion master’s. It models the conversion rules that disqualify applicants who already hold a computing degree, first-class and prerequisite-module bars, and five years of pooled applicant reports under sample-size thresholds for the UK and European programmes. The US programmes are modelled from their published rules only.
ui.2208: What the results mean, in the calculators’ own words, is on the master’s page under How the scoring works, and every results page carries a key to its verdicts. The MBA key gives the model author’s own stated odds, not measured outcomes; the master’s and computing keys give rules and a ranking, never a percentage.
ui.2209: Cross-scale test conversions (GMAT 10th edition, GMAT Focus, GRE) and international grade conversions are percentile-based approximations.
ui.2210: Deadlines. Each programme’s dates were read on the school’s own page on 23 September 2026 for the 2026–27 cycle, and each entry shows when it was last checked. Once the oldest check is more than 120 days old, every results page opens with a warning that the dates are getting old.
